title: How to Become an AI Engineer from a Fullstack Background - Reid Mayo
talk_summary: A syllabus-style career talk mapping a fullstack engineer's path into AI engineering, covering LLM overview, prompt engineering, OpenAI APIs, LangChain, evals, and fine-tuning.

takeaways.technique: Evals as software tests before tuning
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat model/prompt changes like code changes: build a scientific eval process that measures aggregate quality so you can detect regressions before shipping prompt or model changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: evals are basically your software tests before we start fine-tuning blackbox AI models we need a scientific process that can evaluate our changes iteratively

takeaways.what_they_do: Exhaust prompt engineering before fine-tuning, and reuse the best-performing prompts as fine-tuning training data; layer prompt techniques iteratively and measure aggregate quality gains.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fine-tuning quality is often increased by starting with the best performing prompts and using those prompts in your fine-tuning training data

takeaways.technique: Prototype on frontier, scale on cheap fine-tuned open model
takeaways.what_they_do: Ship quickly on a frontier API, collect usage/training data, then fine-tune a smaller open-source model to match or beat it on the target task when cost, latency, or rate limits bite.
takeaways.evidence_quote: prototype and ship a solution quickly using open AIS models start Gathering usage and training data then if the solution needs to start scaling see if you can fine-tune a smaller and cheaper open source model
takeaways.numbers: fine-tuned Llama 2 at $19 matched a frontier model costing ~$244,000 for the same task (speaker's cited case study)

takeaways.what_they_do: Explicitly account for cost-prohibitiveness, latency, rate limiting, and privacy/control as reasons not to depend on one frontier provider alone.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it can be cost prohibitive and you can run into latency or rate limiting issues in production
